Notes on International Affairs | Proceedings - November 1934 Vol. 60/11/381

## Notes on International Affairs 

 Prepared by Professor Allan Westcott, U. S. Naval Academy 

From September 3 to October 3

LEAGUE OF NATIONS ACTIVITIES

Soviet Republic Enters League.—With the strong support of France, as well as Great Britain and Italy, the Soviet Republic on September 18 completed her formal entry into the League of Nations and was at once accorded a permanent seat in the League Council. In the invitation extended to Russia all the nations of Continental Europe joined with the exception of Switzerland, Belgium, Holland, Portugal, and Luxembourg, and all the British commonwealths except the Irish Free State. The final vote in the assembly was 39 in favor of her admission, with 3 opposed and 9 abstentions. The eagerness with which the Soviet government was bent ort thus strengthening its position among the western powers was evident in its disregard of the violent attacks made by some of the smaller states and by its explicit preliminary promise to observe all the obligations incumbent on League members. The only reservation made was that League arbitration pledges should not be applicable to conflicts or questions arising before Russia's entry.

The admission of the Soviet government into the League was regarded not only as of great possible advantage to her in the event of trouble with Japan, but also as a step forward in Foreign Minister Barthou’s plan of lining up the chief Continental powers in support of the status quo in Europe. In connection with this aspect of the matter, the London Daily Herald (Labor), while expressing the hope that Russia’s entry would make for collective security, commented further:

But quite another conception of Geneva has lately been gaining much support. There are those who, flattering themselves that they arc realists, sec in the League a convenient cover for diplomatic scheming of the old type, for forming groups and alliances against particular powers, and for extending the influence of this or that state.

They would use Geneva as a means less of preserving peace than of preparing for war. If that tendency prevails, if the League becomes merely a facade for the operations of old diplomacy, it had almost better be dead.

Work of League Assembly.—Subsequent to the entry of Russia, Afghanistan and Ecuador were also admitted to the League, bringing its total membership to 60 nations. The United States, Brazil, and Costa Rica arc now the only American non-members. Changes in the Council membership included the transfer of China’s non-permanent scat to Turkey, and the election of Chile and re-election of Spain as non-permanent members.

Aside from the accessions noted above, the record of the 13th Assembly and 81st Council sessions was marked by postponements rather than positive action. Little progress was made by the committee engaged in consideration of the Chaco warfare. Efforts to secure stronger guarantees of Austrian independence were carried on mostly outside the regular meetings, and ended in a joint declaration by England, France, and Italy little stronger than those which have gone before. England refused to make definite commitments, Italy opposed surrendering the problem to the feeble hands of the League, and the Little Entente nations objected to any other form of guarantee. Further moves toward disarmament were universally recognized as impracticable, and it was expected that the November meeting of the Council would turn over disarmament problems to a permanent committee. Early in the session Poland threatened to reject League supervision of her treatment of minority peoples, unless such supervision was accepted by other nations, but dropped the matter under pressure from the major powers, who insisted that treaty agreements could not thus be abrogated by unilateral action. As regards the problems created by the coming Saar plebiscite, the special committee headed by Baron Aloisi of Italy took no action save to make provision for a force of neutral police. There was no definite decision to discontinue League rehabilitation work in China, but it was announced that Dr. Rajchmann and other experts formerly engaged there would not return

Eastern Locarno Rejected.—On September 10, Germany in a communication to the interested powers declined participation in the proposed “Eastern Locarno” for stabilizing central Europe, on the professed grounds that the agreement would serve no real need, would be of no profit to her, and would actually involve her in dangerous new commitments. Poland also sent a subsequent communication opposing the plan, especially in view of Germany’s refusal to join, and in view of Poland’s bilateral peace agreements with both Germany and Russia. Poland has recently been further annoyed by the drawing together of the three Baltic states, Esthonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, apparently with Franco-Russian approval, in a pact providing for economic co-operation and opening the way for co-ordination of their foreign policies.

Since even the chief proponents of the Eastern security pact, Commissar Litvinoff and Foreign Minister Barthou, probably had little expectation of German approval and little faith in the pledges if she approved, they are now in a position to go ahead with other plans for safeguarding against German expansion.

EUROPEAN POLITICS

MILITANT ITALY.—Following up Premier Mussolini's warning in August that Italy must stand ready for instant war, a cabinet decree of September 18 laid down a program of military training for each male Italian from his 8th to his 31st year, supplementing his regular 18 months' military service at the age of 21. No immediate danger appears to have prompted this new step toward preparedness, aside from the constant menace of German expansion into Austria. Italy and Albania were reported in September to have come again to friendly relations after the grant of a new Italian loan for armament purchases. Albania in return consented to entry of 10,000 Italian colonists and to continued Italian supervision of the Albanian army. Italy has recently sent military reenforcements to her colonies on the African Red Sea coast, in view of the modernization of the Abyssinian army; but at the close of the month the Italian and Abyssinian governments issued a joint statement of renewed friendship and non-aggression. Also the visit to Rome of Foreign Minister Barthou of France, scheduled for November, is expected to put the recent Franco-Italian rapprochement on a firmer basis and ease the recent friction between Italy and France's Jugoslav ally.

French Constitutional Reforms.—In a radio broadcast on September 24, Premier Doumergue outlined the main governmental reforms advocated by the present French Ministry, designed primarily to strengthen the executive power, along the lines of the British political system. The reforms are:

1. Increased constitutional recognition and authority for the president du conseil, or premier.
2. Power for the premier, upon disagreement with the Chamber, to call new elections without the present cumbersome formalities.
3. The government alone to propose expenditures.
4. The status of civil servants to be defined in constitutional law, with separation of the judiciary from politics.

For the passage of these reforms, the government has a majority in the present Parliament, which is scheduled to convene on November 6, but the opposition is bringing to bear upon them the familiar a arguments against undue concentration of power.

German Church Strife.—There is no better proof of the self-confidence of the Hitler regime in Germany than its willingness to continue the dangerous strife for "Nazification" of the German Evangelical church. On the very day, September 23, when Reichsbishop Ludwig Mueller was consecrated in the Protestant cathedral at Berlin, hostile declarations were read from thousands of pulpits in all parts of Germany. The churches of the two largest South German states, Bavaria and Wurrtbemherg, have held out against unification, but a civil commissioner was given charge of the Wurrttemberg church, and its bishop was put in "protective custody." Decrees have also been prepared to prevent resignations from church membership for the text three years. The ultimate design of the Nazi church leaders, as clearly indicated in their public utterances, is not only to merge the 28 Evangelical State churches, but also to bring both Protestants and Catholics under state control. Prospective pastors will spend at least 6 months in labor camps, where the training will include the use of firearms, and then a year’s grounding in the Nazi philosophy of life.

Fall of Spanish Cabinet.—At the first meeting of the Spanish Cortes on October 1, after its summer recess, the cabinet of Premier Ricardo Samper abruptly resigned, plunging the new Spanish Republic into perhaps the most serious crisis it has yet faced. The immediate cause of the Ministry’s fall was criticism of its weak policy in dealing with Catalan autonomy. Although the Center and Right parties in Spain hold a majority of the scats in the Cortes by virtue of their victory in the last election, the Left extremists threatened revolution in the event of a government under Right control, and they opposed also cither new elections or a coalition ministry representative of all factions. Despite their opposition the veteran former Premier Lerroux was asked to form a new government including representatives of the majority parties.

UNITED STATES AND LATIN AMERICA

American-Soviet Debt Negotiations.—Following an interval in which the American State Department awaited further moves from Moscow, the debt negotiations with the Soviet Ambassador were renewed at the close of September. Little was learned as to new proposals, save the suggestion from Washington that Russia may have withdrawn her request for a direct government loan of $100,000,000, in addition to credits from American exporters for a similar amount. Doubt has been expressed whether, under the proposed scheme of meeting old American claims indirectly by paying excess interest on new loans, the Soviet government will be able to trade here as cheaply as abroad, or whether the American government and people will greatly profit by such trade as may thus develop.

Chaco Peace Plans.—A further effort to intervene in the Chaco warfare, undertaken by Foreign Minister Carlos Saavedra of Argentina with the co-operation of the United States and Brazil, was suddenly suspended in September by the Argentine Minister, and the correspondence was turned over to the League Chaco Committee at Geneva, apparently without the full knowledge or approval of the Brazilian and United States foreign offices. The negotiations, however, were reported as on the verge of another failure. While the League committee is again taking up the problem, operations in the field are likely to be checked by the advent of the rainy season. The Paraguayan plan, as stated by President Ayala, is now to force Bolivia’s evacuation of the entire Chaco territory and then to hold it by strong lines of defense.

FAR EAST

Japan’s Stake in Manchukuo.—The Foreign Policy Report of September 12, 1934, provides a useful survey of the political and economic development of Manchukuo after two years under Japanese guidance. Practically all the capital for the new industrial undertakings in Manchukuo, in coal, oil, mines, forestry, communications, and other fields has come from Japan, and the report questions whether a nation in such financial straits as Japan “can afford to invest such enormous amounts of money in enterprises which, even though economically sound, cannot pay for themselves for decades.” Certainly Manchukuo gives little promise of an outlet for Japan’s excess population.
